# GENERAL GUIDELINES ## Introduction Welcome to HBTF Partner Portal — your gateway to securely accessing externalized banking services via Open Banking APIs. These APIs are designed and published according to Open Banking standards and regulatory requirements, enabling seamless integration with core banking systems using RESTful interfaces. Whether you're building a payment application, financial dashboard, or identity verification flow, our platform empowers you to connect with HBTF in a secure, scalable, and compliant manner. Open Banking APIs serve as digital gateways, allowing third-party developers to build innovative financial solutions around existing banking infrastructure. HBTF Partner Portal ensures these APIs are protected by robust authentication flows, endpoint-level security, and regulatory-grade compliance frameworks — so you can focus on delivering value while we handle the rails. ## 3 Development Modes To support secure and scalable integration, the HBTF Partner Portal offers three distinct modes. Each is designed to match a specific stage of your development and deployment lifecycle. 1. Sandbox Mode The sandbox is your starting point. It provides access to mock APIs that return static or simulated data, allowing you to: - Explore API behavior without impacting real systems - Validate request/response formats - Build and test your application logic safely Why it matters: Sandbox environments are essential in Open Banking projects because they allow developers to iterate quickly, test edge cases, and ensure compliance, all without risking sensitive customer data or triggering real transactions. 2. Certification Mode Once your integration is functionally complete, you’ll move to the certification modes. Here: - You’ll coordinate with HBTF to review your use case - The bank will help determine which API sets are required - You’ll test against the bank’s UAT systems, which return realistic but non-production data This stage ensures your implementation meets HBTF’s security, compliance, and functional standards before going live. 3. Live Mode After successful certification, you’ll be granted access to the live mode. This is where: - Your application interacts with real customer data - Transactions are processed in production - Full audit logging and monitoring are enforced Mode-Specific Credentials Important: Each mode requires its own set of API keys and digital certificates. These must be generated and managed separately to ensure proper isolation and security across development stages. ## Sandbox Integration Steps Follow these steps to get started: 1. Obtain Sandbox Client Credentials - Generate sandbox Client ID and Client Secret from your dashboard. - Go to Client Credentials menu - Click Create Client Credentials - Name your credentials and re-enter your portal password - You will obtain Client ID and Client Secret, PLEASE COPY this information to your local notes, because Client Secret information will only be shown once. - Client ID and Client Secret will be used to authenticate your API call. 2. Obtain Sandbox Digital Certificate Signing To ensure secure communication between partner systems and HBTF’s Open Banking APIs, each partner must request digital certificates signing by uploading a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) file through the portal. This CSR contains your public key and organizational details, which HBTF uses to generate a signed certificate specific to the mode (sandbox, certification, or live). These certificates are essential for establishing mutual TLS (mTLS) connections, verifying the identity of the calling system, and encrypting sensitive data in transit. By isolating certificates per mode, we maintain strict security boundaries and prevent cross-modes leakage or misuse. Get your Sandbox digital certificate signed by Housing Bank. - Go to Certificate menu - Prepare CSR (Certificate Signing Request file from your side) - Click Upload - Upload the CSR file and choose the type of certificate - After it’s uploaded, please wait until the bank signs the certificate 3. Test Sandbox API In order to test HBTF Sandbox API, download the OpenAPI specification from the OpenAPI Collection section below, then import it into Postman or Swagger. Use the Certificate and Client Credentials generated in the portal for authentication. ## Sandbox Test Data The sandbox environment is pre-populated with test data to help you develop and test your integration. Use the following test customers and accounts: ### Test Customers

Use **Retail Customer A** for testing typical account scenarios with multiple active accounts 2. Use **Retail Customer B** for testing closed account handling 3. Use **Business Customer A** for testing corporate customer flows with multiple authorizers ## Get Certified in Certification Mode In the Certification Mode, you will also need to follow the steps of integration just like in Sandbox, which is Obtaining Certification Client Credentials, Obtain Certification Digital Certificate Signing, and test your Certification API. You will need to then coordinate with Housing Bank Personnel, in order to get your certification directly from the bank, outside of the Open Banking platform. ## Get Live Access Once the TPP is granted with the certificate document from Housing Bank, here are the steps to request for Live Access: 1. Click Get Live Access button on the top right 2. You will be redirected to the flow of completing requirements of your company details which include some of the information that have been pre-filled partially during your sign up process. 3. You will be needed to complete the rest of information required in order to request your access 4. Once you complete all the required information, kindly wait for approval from Housing Bank You will be receiving email to get the updates of your Live Request status. ## Go Live After being approved by Housing Bank, you will be getting the access to the Live Mode by choosing the Live Mode in the environment dropdown switch on the top of the portal. You can perform the same exact integration steps which you have done in Sandbox / Certification mode, in order to access the real data and perform the money movement. ## API Overview HBTF Partner Portal APIs are grouped into service categories: Base URLs by Environment

# OTHER GUIDELINES ## OpenAPI Collection Download the OpenAPI Specification here: ## Token Types There are two types of tokens required to call the Open Banking APIs. 1. Access Token 2. Consent Token ### Access Token As a TPP you need to obtain an access token to call the open banking apis which do not require customer consent. Steps to Obtain Access Token 1. Once you complete the signup process successfully, you need to generate client credentials. 2. Use the client credentials from step 1 to generate the access token using `POST /oauth2/token` endpoint. 3. Use the access token generated from step 2 to call the open banking APIs which do not require customer consent. For detailed request/response specifications, parameters, and examples, refer to the **Authentication** section in the API Reference below. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant TPP participant OAuth as OAuth Server participant API as Openbanking API TPP->>OAuth: POST /oauth2/token
(client_id + client_secret) OAuth-->>TPP: Access Token (JWT) TPP->>API: Call API
Authorization: Bearer API-->>TPP: Response ``` ### Consent Token End customer (account holder) consent is required for accessing sensitive account data. Under Open Banking regulations, banks must obtain explicit customer consent before allowing third-party providers to access personal financial information. Why Consent is Required Consent ensures that customers maintain control over their financial data and explicitly authorize which third parties can access their accounts. This is a core principle of Open Banking, designed to protect customer privacy while enabling innovation through secure data sharing with authorized third-party providers. What Data Requires Consent The following types of data require customer consent: - Account details and information - Account balances - Transaction history - Confirmation of funds availability Consent Validity Each consent has a validity window that is automatically set by the system and returned in the consent initiation response: - `ConsentFromDateTime` - When the consent becomes valid - `ConsentToDateTime` - When the consent expires Once a consent expires, the TPP must request a new consent from the customer. Steps to Obtain Consent Token 1. Using the Access Token call the `/consent/initiate` and get a consent id and a deep link. 2. Use the deep link to send the customer to HBTF Iskan mobile banking application 3. After the customer provides consent, obtain the consent token using `POST /consent/{ConsentId}/token` API 4. Use the consent token obtained in step 3 to call the APIs which need customer consent. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant TPP participant API as Openbanking API participant Customer participant Iskan as Iskan App TPP->>API: POST /consent/initiate
(with Access Token) API-->>TPP: consentId + deepLinks
Status: AwaitingAuthorisation TPP->>Customer: Send deepLink Customer->>Iskan: Open Iskan App via deepLink Iskan-->>Customer: Display consent request Customer->>Iskan: Approve consent Iskan->>API: Submit authorization Note over API: Status: Authorised TPP->>API: POST /consent/{ConsentId}/token
(with Access Token) API-->>TPP: Consent Token (JWT) TPP->>API: Call protected API
(Authorization: Bearer consent_token) API-->>TPP: Protected data response ``` ## Endpoint Token Table The following table summarizes which token is required for each API endpoint.

/accounts/{accountId}/transactions/{transactionId} GET Get specific transaction details Consent Token
## Full API Call Flow This section illustrates the complete end-to-end flow for calling a protected API endpoint such as `GET /accounts`. It combines all steps across token types into a single walkthrough. **Steps:** 1. **Obtain Access Token** — authenticate as a TPP using your client credentials against the OAuth server. 2. **Initiate Consent** — use the Access Token to call `POST /consent/initiate` and receive a `consentId` and a deep link. 3. **Customer Authorises** — redirect the customer to the deep link so they can approve consent in the Iskan App. 4. **Obtain Consent Token** — once the consent status is `Authorised`, exchange it for a Consent Token via `POST /consent/{ConsentId}/token`. 5. **Call Protected API** — use the Consent Token to call `GET /accounts` (or any other AIS endpoint). ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant TPP participant OAuth as OAuth Server participant API as Openbanking API participant Customer participant Iskan as Iskan App Note over TPP,OAuth: Step 1 - Obtain Access Token TPP->>OAuth: POST /oauth2/token
(client_id + client_secret) OAuth-->>TPP: Access Token (JWT) Note over TPP,API: Step 2 - Initiate Consent TPP->>API: POST /consent/initiate
(Authorization: Bearer access_token) API-->>TPP: consentId + deepLinks
Status: AwaitingAuthorisation Note over TPP,Iskan: Step 3 - Customer Authorises TPP->>Customer: Send deepLink Customer->>Iskan: Open Iskan App via deepLink Iskan-->>Customer: Display consent request Customer->>Iskan: Approve consent Iskan->>API: Submit authorization Note over API: Status: Authorised Note over TPP,API: Step 4 - Obtain Consent Token TPP->>API: POST /consent/{ConsentId}/token
(Authorization: Bearer access_token) API-->>TPP: Consent Token (JWT) Note over TPP,API: Step 5 - Call Protected API TPP->>API: GET /accounts
(Authorization: Bearer consent_token) API-->>TPP: List of customer accounts ``` ## Consent Overview ### What is Consent? Consent is a regulatory requirement under Open Banking frameworks that ensures account holders explicitly authorize Third-Party Providers (TPPs) to access their financial data. It serves as a digital agreement between the customer, the bank, and the TPP, defining what data can be accessed and for how long. The consent mechanism protects customer privacy while enabling innovation in financial services. All consents are managed through secure authentication flows and can be revoked by customers at any time. ### Consent Statuses A consent progresses through various states during its lifecycle:
Status Description Next Actions
AwaitingAuthorisation Consent has been created and is pending customer approval Customer must approve or reject via HBTF Iskan app
FirstLevelAuthorised Partial approval received (applicable for corporate accounts requiring multiple approvers) Awaiting additional authorization levels
Authorised Consent has been fully approved by the customer TPP can exchange consent for access token
Rejected Customer declined the consent request TPP must initiate a new consent if needed
Revoked Previously granted consent has been revoked by customer or bank TPP must initiate a new consent if continued access is needed
Expired Consent validity period has ended TPP must initiate a new consent
### Consent Lifecycle The consent flow varies depending on the customer type (RETAIL or CORPORATE). #### Retail Customer Flow For retail customers, consent requires single-level authorization: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant TPP participant API as Openbanking API participant Customer participant Iskan as Iskan App TPP->>API: POST /consent/initiate
(CustomerType: RETAIL) API-->>TPP: consentId + deepLinks
Status: AwaitingAuthorisation TPP->>Customer: Redirect to deepLink Customer->>Iskan: Open Iskan App Iskan-->>Customer: Display consent request
(TPP name, permissions, validity) Customer->>Iskan: Approve or Reject Iskan->>API: Submit authorization Note over API: Status: Authorised (if approved)
or Rejected TPP->>API: POST /consent/{id}/token API-->>TPP: Consent Token (JWT) TPP->>API: Call protected APIs
(accounts, balances, transactions) ``` #### Corporate Customer Flow For corporate customers, consent requires two-level authorization (multiple approvers): ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant TPP participant API as Openbanking API participant Approver1 as First Approver participant Approver2 as Second Approver participant Iskan as Iskan App TPP->>API: POST /consent/initiate
(CustomerType: CORPORATE) API-->>TPP: consentId + deepLinks
Status: AwaitingAuthorisation TPP->>Approver1: Redirect to deepLink Approver1->>Iskan: Open Iskan App Iskan-->>Approver1: Display consent request
(requires 2 approvers) Approver1->>Iskan: Approve (First Level) Iskan->>API: Submit first authorization Note over API: Status: FirstLevelAuthorised TPP->>Approver2: Redirect to deepLink Approver2->>Iskan: Open Iskan App Iskan-->>Approver2: Display pending consent
(already has 1 approval) Approver2->>Iskan: Approve (Second Level) Iskan->>API: Submit second authorization Note over API: Status: Authorised TPP->>API: POST /consent/{id}/token API-->>TPP: Consent Token (JWT) TPP->>API: Call protected APIs
(accounts, balances, transactions) ``` **Note**: For corporate customers, if any approver rejects the consent at any level, the consent status becomes "Rejected" and the process terminates. Detailed Step-by-Step Process:
Step Actor Action Details Applies To
1 TPP → Openbanking API POST /consent/initiate Initiate consent with Access Token. Specify CustomerType (RETAIL or CORPORATE) and DeviceType. Both
2 Openbanking API → TPP consentId + deepLinks Receive consentId and device-specific deep links. Status: AwaitingAuthorisation Both
3 TPP → Customer/Approver Redirect to deepLink Direct the customer/first approver to the deep link based on their device type. Both
4 Customer/Approver → Iskan App Open Iskan App Customer/approver opens the Iskan mobile banking app via the deep link. Both
5 Iskan App → Customer/Approver Display consent request App shows consent details: TPP name, permissions, validity period. For corporate, indicates multiple approvers required. Both
6 Customer/Approver → Iskan App Approve or Reject Customer/first approver reviews and either approves or rejects the consent request. Both
7 Iskan App → Openbanking API Submit authorization Retail: Status changes to "Authorised" (if approved) or "Rejected"
Corporate: Status changes to "FirstLevelAuthorised" (if approved) or "Rejected"		 Both
8 TPP → Second Approver Redirect to deepLink Direct the second approver to the same consent deep link. Corporate Only
9 Second Approver → Iskan App Open Iskan App Second approver opens Iskan app and sees the pending consent (already has 1 approval). Corporate Only
10 Second Approver → Iskan App Approve or Reject (Second Level) Second approver reviews and either approves or rejects. Corporate Only
11 Iskan App → Openbanking API Submit second authorization Status changes to "Authorised" (if approved) or "Rejected" Corporate Only
12 TPP → Openbanking API POST /consent/{id}/token Exchange consent for Consent Token (JWT). Only works when status is "Authorised". Both
13 Openbanking API → TPP Consent Token (JWT) TPP receives the token required to call protected APIs. Both
14 TPP → Openbanking API Call protected APIs Use the Consent Token to call protected APIs (accounts, balances, transactions). Both
**Key Differences:** - **Retail customers**: Single approval moves consent directly from "AwaitingAuthorisation" to "Authorised" - **Corporate customers**: Requires two approvals. First approval moves consent to "FirstLevelAuthorised", second approval moves it to "Authorised" - Both approvers for corporate accounts must approve via the same consent deep link - If any approver rejects at any level, the consent immediately becomes "Rejected" ### Date and Time Formats All date/time fields in the API use **RFC 3339** format (ISO 8601 compatible). **Format**: `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` or `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS+00:00` **Examples**: - `2026-02-15T10:30:00Z` (UTC timezone) - `2026-02-15T13:30:00+03:00` (with timezone offset of +3 hours) **Common Fields Using This Format**:
Field Name Context Description
ConsentFromDateTime Consent When consent becomes valid
ConsentToDateTime Consent When consent expires
CreationDateTime Resources When resource was created
StatusUpdateDateTime Resources When status was last updated
BookingDateTime Transactions When transaction was booked to account
ValueDateTime Transactions When transaction value is applied
TransactionDateTime Transactions When transaction was performed
**Notes**: - All timestamps are returned in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) with 'Z' suffix - When sending timestamps in requests, you can use either UTC or include a timezone offset - The API automatically converts all timestamps to UTC for processing - Timezone information is preserved in the response when explicitly provided ### Consent Request Fields When initiating a consent, the following fields must be provided:
Field Type Description Required
CustomerType String Type of customer: RETAIL or CORPORATE Yes
DeviceType String Customer's device platform: Android, IOS, or Huawei Yes
Metadata Object Additional key-value data for TPP reference No
### Consent Response Fields When you successfully initiate a consent, the API returns the following fields:
Field Type Description
ConsentId String Unique identifier for the consent
CreationDateTime Timestamp When the consent was created
Status String Current status (typically "AwaitingAuthorisation")
Permissions Array List of permissions granted (e.g., ReadAccounts, ReadBalances, ReadTransactions)
ConsentFromDateTime Timestamp When the consent becomes valid (system-generated)
ConsentToDateTime Timestamp When the consent expires (system-generated)
Links Array Device-specific deep links for different platforms (Android, iOS, Huawei)
### APIs Requiring Consent Token The following APIs require a valid Consent Token (obtained from `/consent/{ConsentId}/token` after customer authorization): Account Service - `GET /accounts` - List customer accounts - `GET /accounts/{accountAddress}` - Get specific account details - `GET /accounts/{accountId}/balances` - Retrieve account balances - `POST /accounts/{accountId}/CAF` - Confirmation of Availability of Funds > **Note**: `accountAddress` and `accountId` both refer to the account number. The naming differs by endpoint but the value is the same — use the account number returned from `GET /accounts`. Transaction Service - `GET /accounts/{accountId}/transactions` - Retrieve transaction history - `GET /accounts/{accountId}/transactions/{transactionId}` - Get specific transaction details ## HTTP Response Code
Code Label Description
200 OK Processing is successful
400 BAD REQUEST The request payload has a missing parameter and/or invalid format
401 UNAUTHORIZED Authentication failed — missing, invalid, or expired access/consent token
403 FORBIDDEN Authenticated but insufficient permissions or the organization is not authorized for the requested resource
404 NOT FOUND The requested resource does not exist
500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR An unexpected error occurred while processing the request
## Error Response Format All API error responses follow a consistent JSON structure: ```json { "id": "abc123-trace-id", "code": "http.request.invalid", "desc": "Invalid request parameter", "error": [ { "code": "MISSING_FIELD", "desc": "customerType is required" } ] } ```
Field Type Description
id String Correlation/trace ID for the request. Useful for debugging with the HBTF support team.
code String Machine-readable error code identifying the error category
desc String Human-readable description of the error
error Array List of specific error details (may contain multiple validation errors)
Common Error Codes
HTTP Status Error Code Description

401 http.auth.header.missing Authorization header is not included in the request
401 http.auth.token.invalid The provided authentication token is invalid or the user is not authorized

401 http.auth.consent.not_authorised The consent exists but has not been authorised by the customer
401 http.auth.consent.expired The consent has expired and a new consent must be initiated

404 resource.notFound The requested resource could not be found
500 server.error An internal server error occurred
## JAdES Baseline-B HTTP Signature Guide This document explains how a TPP generates a JWS signature (JAdES Baseline-B) and attaches it to an HTTP API request. It covers: - Certificate onboarding - Request preparation - Digest calculation - Canonicalization - Protected header creation - Signature generation - Final JWS assembly --- ### 1️⃣ Certificate Onboarding (One-Time Setup) **Step 1.1 – Generate CSR and Private Key** The TPP generates a private key and CSR locally. **Artifacts Created** - `jades_private.key` → **Private key (must be kept secret)** - `jades.csr` → Certificate Signing Request ⚠️ The private key must never be uploaded or shared. JAdES Baseline-B requires a strong asymmetric key.\ The recommended key type is **RSA 2048 or higher**. **Generate RSA 2048 Private Key** ``` bash openssl genrsa -out jades_private.key 2048 ``` **Create CSR (Certificate Signing Request)** ``` bash openssl req -new \ -key jades_private.key \ -out jades.csr \ -sha256 ``` You will be prompted to enter certificate subject details. **Step 1.2 -- Upload CSR to Bank Portal** 1. Navigate to **Certificate → Upload** 2. Upload `jades.csr` 3. Select **Certificate Type: JAdES** 4. Submit for signing **Step 1.3 -- Download Signed Certificate** After approval, download: jades-cert.pem This certificate is used to: - Prove TPP identity - Generate the certificate thumbprint - Allow the Bank to verify signatures --- ### 2️⃣ Certificate Thumbprint Generation **Thumbprint Rules** Property Value ---------------- ------------------------- Hash Algorithm SHA-256 Encoding Base64URL (no padding) Input DER-encoded certificate This value is included in the protected header: ``` json "x5t#S256": "" ``` --- ### 3️⃣ HTTP Request Preparation Prepare the HTTP request exactly as it will be sent: - HTTP Method (GET / POST / PUT) - Full request path (including query parameters) - Headers - Optional JSON body ⚠️ Any change after signing will invalidate the signature. --- ### 4️⃣ Digest Header (Only If Body Exists) Request Type Digest Required ---------------------- ----------------- GET (no body) ❌ No POST / PUT with body ✅ Yes If a body exists: 1. Compute SHA-256 hash of raw request body 2. Base64-encode using **standard Base64** 3. Prefix with `SHA-256=` Format: Digest: SHA-256= --- ### 5️⃣ Select Headers to Sign (`sigD.pars`) Typical signed headers: (request-target) host digest (only if body exists) content-type (recommended) ⚠️ The order must be preserved and reused consistently. --- ### 6️⃣ Build Canonical Signing String Example: (request-target): post /payments?type=instant host: api.bank.com digest: SHA-256=abc123... content-type: application/json Rules: - Method must be lowercase - Header names must be lowercase - Use `\n` between lines - No trailing spaces --- ### 7️⃣ Create JWS Protected Header ``` json { "alg": "RS256", "b64": true, "crit": ["sigT", "sigD", "b64"], "sigT": "2026-01-26T12:45:30Z", "sigD": { "pars": [ "(request-target)", "host", "digest", "content-type" ], "mId": "http://uri.etsi.org/19182/HttpHeaders", "hashM": "S256", "hashV": [ "" ] }, "x5t#S256": "" } ``` --- ### 8️⃣ Encode Protected Header EncodedProtectedHeader = Base64URL(JSON) --- ### 9️⃣ Build Signing Input EncodedProtectedHeader + "." + CanonicalSigningString --- ### 🔟 Generate Digital Signature 1. Hash signing input using SHA-256\ 2. Sign using TPP private key (RSA)\ 3. Encode signature using Base64URL (no padding) ```{=html} ``` EncodedSignature = Base64URL(SignatureBytes) --- ### 1️⃣1️⃣ Create Final JWS (Detached Payload) EncodedProtectedHeader .. EncodedSignature ⚠️ Note the double dot (`..`) --- ### 1️⃣2️⃣ Attach JWS to HTTP Request Required header: X-JWS-Signature: Final HTTP structure: Headers: - X-JWS-Signature - Digest (if body exists) - Content-Type Body: - Original JSON payload (unchanged) --- ### ✅ Summary To generate a valid JAdES Baseline-B signature: 1. Prepare request 2. Generate digest (if needed) 3. Build canonical string 4. Create protected header 5. Encode header 6. Sign input 7. Assemble detached JWS 8. Attach `X-JWS-Signature` header --- ### 💻 Core Java Example – JAdES HTTP Client This section provides a **Core Java (no framework)** example demonstrating how to generate and attach a **JAdES Baseline-B HTTP signature** (`X-JWS-Signature`) to an API request. The implementation follows the same signing logic as the official Golang client: - SHA-256 digest calculation - Canonical string construction - `sigD.pars` processing - `hashV` calculation - RS256 digital signature - Detached JWS format (`header..signature`) This example uses only: - `java.net.http.HttpClient` - `java.security` - `java.util.Base64` No Spring or external frameworks are required. **What This Script Does** 1. Builds the HTTP request 2. Calculates `Digest` header (if body exists) 3. Constructs canonical signing string 4. Builds protected JWS header 5. Calculates `sigD.hashV` values 6. Signs using RSA-SHA256 7. Creates detached JWS (`..`) 8. Sends request with `X-JWS-Signature` header **Requirements** - Java 11+ - RSA private key (PKCS8 format) - Certificate thumbprint (`x5t#S256`) - Valid OAuth Access Token **Sample Usage** Update the following values before running: - `YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN` - `YOUR_CERT_THUMBPRINT` - `private_key_pkcs8.pem` - Target API URL **Core Java Implementation** ```java import java.io.*; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpClient; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.security.*; import java.security.interfaces.RSAPrivateKey; import java.security.spec.PKCS8EncodedKeySpec; import java.time.Instant; import java.util.*; import java.util.Base64; public class JadesHttpClient { /* ================= CONFIG ================= */ static class Config { String authToken; RSAPrivateKey privateKey; String thumbprint; public Config(String authToken, RSAPrivateKey privateKey, String thumbprint) { this.authToken = authToken; this.privateKey = privateKey; this.thumbprint = thumbprint; } } /* ================= MAIN ================= */ public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { RSAPrivateKey privateKey = loadPrivateKey("private_key_pkcs8.pem"); String thumbprint = "YOUR_CERT_THUMBPRINT"; Config config = new Config( "YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN", privateKey, thumbprint ); String url = "https://sandbox.openbanking.hbtf.com/institution/SSTs"; String method = "GET"; String body = null; List signedHeaders = Arrays.asList( "(request-target)", "host" );
